data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Most people learn fractions as pizza slices. Today you learn them as **places** — spots on a number line. This is the version that keeps working when the math gets bigger.

1. Read **The Space Between 0 and 1**.
2. Learn the words in the **Glossary**, then win the **Word Scramble**.
3. Do the **Practice Problems** one at a time. Say each answer out loud before checking.
4. Sort the cards in **Bigger, Smaller, or Equal to One-Half?**
5. Take the quiz — question 3 catches almost everyone.
6. Read **Fraction Questions Kids Actually Ask** if something still feels strange.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Space Between** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Design Challenge: A Number Line for the Hallway** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

Tip: if a fraction confuses you, draw the number line. Every single time. Drawing is not cheating; it is what mathematicians actually do. ✏️📏

objectives.label: I drew a number line to solve at least one problem

history.title: The Space Between 0 and 1
history.data:
## The Space Between 0 and 1

Count out loud: 1, 2, 3, 4. Easy. Now count what is *between* 1 and 2.

There is a whole world in there, and fractions are how we name the places inside it.

Start with a number line. Put 0 at the left and 1 at the right. Now cut the space between them into **4 equal pieces**. The cuts land on new places, and each place has a name: one-fourth, two-fourths, three-fourths. Written as numbers: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4.

The bottom number — the **denominator** — tells you *how many equal pieces the whole was cut into*. The top number — the **numerator** — tells you *how many of those pieces you counted from zero*.

So 3/4 is not a pizza. It is a **location**. Walk three of the four steps from 0 toward 1 and stop. That is where 3/4 lives.

Here is where the number line earns its keep. Look at 2/4. Now look at 1/2. They land on the exact same spot. Same location, two names. That is what **equivalent fractions** means — different words, same place, like a friend who goes by a nickname.

The number line also fixes the most common fraction mistake. Which is bigger, 1/4 or 1/8? Many people say 1/8, because 8 is bigger than 4. But look: cutting the space into 8 pieces makes each piece *smaller*. So 1/8 sits closer to 0, and 1/4 is bigger. **More pieces means smaller pieces.** The number line shows you that instantly, and it never lies.

One more thing. Fractions do not stop at 1. Keep going: 5/4 is one step past 1. Fractions are just numbers, and the number line goes on forever in both directions. Once you see fractions as places instead of slices, they stop being a special weird topic and become ordinary numbers — which is exactly what they are.

data.def: A number that names equal parts of a whole — it can sit between whole numbers or land right on one.
The top number — how many equal pieces you counted.
The bottom number — how many equal pieces the whole was cut into.
Equal in value — two fractions that land on the same spot.
The complete amount, from 0 to 1 on the number line.
The same size or the same amount.
One single piece — like 1/4 is one unit of a fourth.
The two equal pieces you get by cutting a whole in two.
The four equal pieces you get by cutting a whole into four.
To decide which of two numbers is bigger, smaller, or equal.

data.title: Remember the Space Between
data.instructions: Each card locks in one idea from The Space Between 0 and 1. Look at the example aid, make it your own, and tell how it helps you on the number line.
data.sourceExcerpt: The bottom number, the denominator, tells you how many equal pieces the whole was cut into. The top number, the numerator, tells you how many of those pieces you counted from zero. 2/4 and 1/2 land on the exact same spot. More pieces means smaller pieces.

cards.target: Denominator on the bottom tells the pieces; numerator on top tells the count
essentialFacts: The denominator (bottom) tells how many equal pieces the whole was cut into.
The numerator (top) tells how many pieces you counted from zero.
3/4 means walk three of the four steps from 0 toward 1.
cards.aiExample: Denominator = Down = how many pieces. Numerator = Number you counted. D is down; N is the number of steps you took.
cards.mapping: Both hooks use the first letter of the word: D for down puts the denominator on the bottom, and N for number reminds you the numerator is the count.
cards.scaffoldStarter: D is for ____, so the denominator is on the ____. N is for ____, so the numerator tells ____.
scaffoldSteps: Say each word and listen for its first letter.
Attach down to the bottom number and number to the top.
coachPrompts: Using your hook, which number changes when you cut the line into more pieces?
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your hook stop you from mixing up the two numbers?

hookFact.text: 3/4 is not a pizza. It is a location: walk three of the four steps from 0 toward 1 and stop.

cards.target: More pieces means smaller pieces: 1/8 is smaller than 1/4
essentialFacts: Cutting the space from 0 to 1 into 8 pieces makes each piece smaller than cutting it into 4.
So 1/8 sits closer to 0, and 1/4 is bigger.
This fixes the most common fraction mistake: thinking 1/8 is bigger because 8 is bigger.
cards.aiExample: Bigger bottom, smaller bite: more pieces means each is slight.
cards.mapping: The rhyme puts the trap and the fix in one breath: a bigger denominator (bottom) means a smaller piece (bite), which is the opposite of what your whole-number brain expects.
scaffoldSteps: Say the rule in plain words.
Find two words that rhyme for bottom and piece.
coachPrompts: Does your rhyme work when the top numbers are the same but the bottoms are different?
cards.studentPrompt: Write your own two-line rhyme for the pieces rule.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your rhyme help you when your brain says 8 is bigger than 4?

hookFact.text: Many people say 1/8 is bigger than 1/4 because 8 is bigger than 4. The number line shows you instantly that it is not, and it never lies.

cards.target: Equivalent fractions: same spot, two names
essentialFacts: 2/4 and 1/2 land on the exact same spot on the number line.
Equivalent fractions are different names for the same place.
4/8 and 3/6 are also names for that halfway spot.
cards.aiExample: Picture one friend standing exactly halfway down a hallway. Her name tag says 1/2 on one side and 2/4 on the other. Two tags, one person, one spot.
cards.mapping: The friend is the location, the tags are the names, and the single spot in the hallway is the number line, so equivalent means two tags on one person, not two people.
cards.scaffoldStarter: One person stands at ____. Her tags say ____ and ____.
scaffoldSteps: Draw or picture a hallway from 0 to 1.
Put one person at the halfway spot with two name tags.
Add a third tag that also belongs there.
coachPrompts: Could 3/4 be a tag on the same person? Why not?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own one-spot, two-names picture.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your picture show what equivalent means?

hookFact.text: Same location, two names, like a friend who goes by a nickname.

problems.question: A number line runs from 0 to 1 and is cut into 4 equal pieces. Which fraction sits at the very first cut mark after 0?

steps.explanation: The denominator is 4 because the whole was cut into 4 equal pieces.
The first mark after 0 is one piece from the start, so the numerator is 1.

problems.realWorld: A running lap divided into four quarters: the first quarter mark.

problems.question: Which is bigger: 1/4 or 1/8? Explain using pieces.

steps.explanation: Cutting the same whole into 8 pieces makes each piece smaller than cutting it into 4.
So one piece out of 8 is closer to zero than one piece out of 4.

problems.realWorld: Sharing one candy bar with 4 friends versus 8 friends — bigger group, smaller share.

problems.question: Name a fraction that lands on the exact same spot as 1/2 when the line is cut into fourths.

steps.explanation: Cut 0 to 1 into 4 equal pieces and walk 2 of them.
You stop exactly halfway, which is where 1/2 is.
So 2/4 and 1/2 are equivalent — same place, two names.

problems.realWorld: Half a sandwich is the same as two quarter-pieces of that sandwich.

problems.question: On a line cut into thirds, where does 3/3 land?

steps.explanation: The denominator 3 means 3 equal pieces make one whole.
The numerator 3 means you walk all 3 pieces.
Walking every piece brings you to the whole, which is 1.

problems.realWorld: Eating all three slices of a three-slice pie means you ate one whole pie.

problems.question: A line is cut into fourths and continues past 1. Where does 5/4 land?

steps.explanation: Four fourths get you exactly to 1.
The fifth fourth is one more piece beyond that.
So 5/4 sits one fourth to the right of 1.

problems.realWorld: Running one full lap plus a quarter of the next one.

problems.question: Order these from smallest to largest: 3/4, 1/4, 2/4.

steps.explanation: All three have the same denominator, so the pieces are the same size.
When piece size matches, more pieces means farther from 0.
Counting up the numerators gives 1/4, then 2/4, then 3/4.

problems.realWorld: Three water bottles filled to different quarter marks, lined up shortest to tallest.

Check Your Thinking

questions.question: What does the DENOMINATOR of a fraction tell you?
options: How many equal pieces the whole was cut into
How many pieces you are counting
How far the fraction is from zero
Whether the fraction is big or small
questions.correctAnswer: How many equal pieces the whole was cut into

questions.question: On a number line from 0 to 1 cut into 8 equal pieces, where is 4/8?
options: Just before 1, near the right end
Exactly halfway between 0 and 1
Just after 0, near the left end
Past 1, to the right of the whole

questions.question: Which is LARGER: 1/6 or 1/3?
options: 1/6, because 6 is a bigger number than 3
They are equal because both numerators are 1
1/3, because fewer pieces means bigger pieces
You cannot compare them without a calculator
questions.correctAnswer: 1/3, because fewer pieces means bigger pieces

questions.question: The reading says 3/4 is a location, not a pizza slice. What does that mean?
options: It only works when you are measuring distance along a road or a ruler
Pizza cannot be used to show fractions, because slices are never truly equal
It means 3/4 is not really a number, just a picture of a place
It is a specific spot on the number line, three-fourths of the way from 0 to 1
questions.correctAnswer: It is a specific spot on the number line, three-fourths of the way from 0 to 1

questions.question: Your classmate says '1/8 must be bigger than 1/4 because 8 is bigger than 4.' Draw or describe a number line that shows why this is wrong.
questions.expectedAnswer: Cut 0 to 1 into 4 pieces and mark 1/4; then cut the same line into 8 pieces and mark 1/8. The 1/8 mark is closer to 0. More pieces make each piece smaller, so 1/4 is larger.

questions.question: Explain in your own words what makes two fractions equivalent.
questions.expectedAnswer: They land on the exact same spot on the number line — the same amount with two different names, like 2/4 and 1/2.

reflections.text: Where do you see fractions outside of math class? Name two real places.
Which was easier for you: thinking of fractions as slices or as places on a line? Why?

data.question: Why do we even need fractions? 🤷
data.answer: Because almost nothing in real life comes in whole numbers. Half an hour, three-quarters of a cup, a quarter mile. Whole numbers alone cannot measure the world.

data.question: Is 1/2 the same as 0.5?
data.answer: Yes! Same location on the number line, two ways of writing it. Decimals are just fractions where the denominator is always 10, 100, 1000, and so on.

data.question: Can the top number be bigger than the bottom? 🤔
data.answer: Absolutely. 5/4 just means you walked five fourth-sized steps, which takes you past 1. Those are called improper fractions, though there is nothing improper about them.

data.question: Why does my brain say 1/8 is bigger than 1/4?
data.answer: Because 8 is bigger than 4, and your brain is pattern-matching to whole numbers. It is the single most common fraction mistake — which is why the number line is worth drawing every time.

data.question: What is the biggest fraction between 0 and 1?
data.answer: There is no biggest one, and that is the wild part. You can always get closer to 1: 99/100, then 999/1000, forever. Between any two fractions there is always another.

data.question: Do fractions go on the negative side of the number line too?
data.answer: They do — negative one-half sits exactly as far left of 0 as one-half sits right of it. You will work with those more in later grades.

history.title: Design Challenge: A Number Line for the Hallway
history.meta: 3rd-4th Grade • Design brief • a walkable fraction line

data.title: A Number Line for the Hallway
data.instructions: Design a number line on the hallway floor that students can walk from 0 to 1 and beyond, with the fraction marks placed so they are truly equal. Then test it: do two names land on the same spot?
data.fitReason: The reading insists fractions are places. A number line big enough to walk makes equal pieces, equivalent names, and 5/4 into something students measure with their feet.

brief.context: Your teacher has painter's tape, a measuring tape, index cards, and permission to use a 4-meter stretch of hallway floor for a week. Younger classes will walk it too.
brief.audience: Your class and a second-grade class that will walk the line
brief.drivingQuestion: How do we place the marks for fourths, halves, and eighths so every piece is truly equal, and how do we show that 1/2, 2/4, and 4/8 are one spot?
brief.seedDirection: Decide how long 0 to 1 will be first. Every other mark is that length divided into equal pieces, so measure, do not guess.
lockedLessonFacts: The denominator tells how many equal pieces the whole was cut into; the numerator tells how many you counted from zero.
2/4 and 1/2 land on the exact same spot: equivalent fractions are two names for one place.
More pieces means smaller pieces: 1/8 is closer to 0 than 1/4.
Fractions do not stop at 1: 5/4 is one fourth past 1.
openQuestions: How long should 0 to 1 be so that eighths are still far enough apart to stand on?
How do we make sure our pieces are equal, not just close?
Where do we put 5/4 if the hallway ends?
How will a second grader know that two cards at one spot are the same place?
stakeholders: Second graders who will walk the line
The custodian who removes the tape later
Students in wheelchairs who need the marks readable from the side
criteria: Every fourth is the same measured length, and every eighth is exactly half a fourth
1/2, 2/4, and 4/8 share one mark with all three cards
At least one mark past 1 is placed and labeled
A second grader can walk to 3/4 without help using your labels
constraints: Tape only, no marker on the floor
The line must leave room for people to pass
Cards must be readable from standing height
Built and tested in one class period
brief.deliverable: A plan drawing with measured distances, the built line, a test record (three second graders asked to walk to 3/4, 1/2, and 5/4, and where they stopped), and one sentence about what you would change.

parallelExample.context: A class built a number line but put the halfway mark by eye.
parallelExample.move: When they measured, 1/2 was 10 centimeters off, so 2/4 and 1/2 landed on different spots and the second graders thought they were different numbers. They remeasured, fixed the mark, and taped both cards to one spot.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows why measuring matters: equal pieces are what make equivalent fractions land together.

supports.frameStarter: Our whole is ____ long. Each fourth is ____, each eighth is ____. The mark for 1/2 has cards for ____ and ____.
frameChoices: Build fourths first, then split each into eighths
Build eighths first, then label every second one as a fourth
Add a second color of tape for marks past 1
Add thirds in a different color to compare piece sizes
coachPrompts: How do you know your fourths are equal without trusting your eyes?
What happens to a second grader's walk if one piece is longer than the others?
Where would 1/3 go, and why is it not on any of your marks?

data.coachHint: Measure the whole, divide, measure again. Equal pieces are the entire idea.
